summary.text: Linear algebra studies vector spaces, sets whose elements can be added together and scaled by numbers, along with the linear maps between them.
It is central to almost all areas of mathematics, and it is used in most sciences, in engineering and in computing.
Its roots lie in solving systems of linear equations: Gaussian elimination appears in an ancient Chinese text, and Descartes's coordinates in 1637 turned lines and planes into linear equations.

facts.label: Matrix named
facts.value: Sylvester introduced the term matrix in 1848

facts.label: Matrix multiplication
facts.value: Cayley introduced it, with the inverse matrix, in 1856

facts.label: Vector space defined
facts.value: Peano gave the first modern definition in 1888

facts.label: What vectors can be
facts.value: Tuples, sequences, functions, polynomials or matrices

facts.label: Oldest method
facts.value: Gaussian elimination appears in an ancient Chinese text

items.prompt: Two lines are drawn on graph paper using coordinates. Finding the spot where they cross amounts to what task?

options.label: Measuring the angle between them
Computing a single matrix
Solving a system of linear equations
Finding an isomorphism of vector spaces

items.explain: In Cartesian geometry lines and planes are represented by linear equations, so computing their intersections amounts to solving systems of linear equations.

items.prompt: A scientist studies a curved, nonlinear system. How can linear algebra still help near one point?

options.label: A line models the curve's local behavior, and that can be analyzed
It proves the system is secretly linear everywhere
It cannot help, since it only handles straight lines
It replaces the whole curve with a single average value

items.explain: Linear algebra is often used for first-order approximations: the derivative gives the slope of a line that models the local behavior.

items.prompt: A student believes vectors must be arrows. Which statement is accurate?

options.label: Only arrows and lists of numbers can be vectors
Vectors can be numbers but never functions
Arrows count as vectors only when scaled by whole numbers
Functions and polynomials can be vectors too

items.explain: The elements of a vector space are called vectors, and they can be tuples, sequences, functions, polynomials or matrices.

items.prompt: A set is called a vector space if its elements can be combined in two particular ways. What are they?

options.label: Dividing two elements, and taking a square root
Adding two elements, and scaling an element by a number
Multiplying two elements, and inverting an element
Comparing two elements, and putting them in order

items.explain: A vector space has vector addition and scalar multiplication.

items.prompt: Two vector spaces are linked by an isomorphism, so mathematicians call them essentially the same. In what sense?

options.label: Every element of one is literally an element of the other
They are written with the same symbols and notation
No vector-space property can tell them apart
They always contain the same finite number of elements

items.explain: An isomorphism preserves linear structure, so the two spaces cannot be distinguished by using vector space properties.

items.prompt: A linear map sends some inputs all to the zero vector. What is the set of those inputs called?

options.label: The kernel of the map
The range of the map
The field of scalars
The isomorphism itself

items.explain: The elements that are mapped to the zero vector form the kernel of the map, while the range (or image) is what the map reaches.
